Memo: Local AI hardware versus better utilisation

To: Platform and ML engineering leads
From: Infrastructure review
Re: Whether to buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of what we own

Recommendation up front: do not make a large hardware purchase yet. Run a focused utilisation and latency review for the next two quarters, fix the obvious waste, and only then buy capacity for the workloads that remain genuinely constrained. If the review shows a stable, growing gap in a specific class of inference or fine-tuning work, a limited purchase is justified. If it shows that most GPUs are idle, oversized, or duplicated, the cheaper and safer path is better scheduling, batching, autoscaling, and clearer ownership.

The case for buying more hardware is understandable. Local inference is attractive because it keeps data inside our environment, avoids per-token external pricing, and can give predictable latency for sensitive workloads. If demand is rising, waiting for utilisation to improve could feel like leaving performance on the table. But hardware is a blunt instrument. It improves the ceiling, not the average. A new GPU does not help if the job queue is poorly shaped, if models are loaded and unloaded too often, if small requests are sent one at a time, or if several teams each run near-identical stacks.

The case for utilisation is stronger. Our current estate appears to have a mix of always-on services, bursty batch jobs, and experiments that never quite graduate. That pattern wastes money in several ways. Idle accelerators still consume power, cooling, maintenance attention, and engineering time. Oversized instances force teams to pay for headroom they do not use. Duplicated deployments make it harder to reason about latency, capacity, and failure modes. Opportunity cost matters too: every dollar spent on hardware is a dollar not spent on observability, data quality, model evaluation, or developer tooling. Those investments may not feel as dramatic as a new rack, but they often reduce the need for hardware.

Latency deserves special attention. Buying more hardware can reduce queueing delay, but it can also mask the real cause of slow responses. If p95 latency is high because requests are serialised, models are cold-started, or prompts are too large, more GPUs will only move the bottleneck. A better path is to measure where time is spent: queue wait, model load, prefill, decode, retrieval, post-processing, and network hops. Once we know the dominant term, the fix may be batching, caching, smaller models, quantization, better routing, or a different serving pattern rather than more silicon.

Reliability is another reason to be cautious. More hardware increases the number of components, drivers, containers, and failure modes. It can also create pressure to keep everything running, which is not always wise. Utilisation work improves reliability by making the system easier to understand: fewer orphaned services, clearer ownership, better telemetry, and more predictable capacity. That is not a guarantee of uptime, but it is a better foundation.

Reversibility is important. Software changes are comparatively reversible: we can change batch sizes, routing rules, model choices, or deployment schedules and observe the effect. Hardware purchases are less reversible. Once bought, capacity is hard to resell quickly, and depreciation does not care whether demand changes. A modest purchase can be reversed through resale or redeployment, but a large one is a commitment. That asymmetry argues for evidence before spend.

Uncertainty is real. Demand may grow faster than expected. Some workloads may be latency-sensitive enough that utilisation improvements cannot meet targets. Local hardware may be the only acceptable option for regulated data. We should not pretend otherwise. The right move is therefore not “never buy,” but “buy after proof.”

A practical path is to instrument the estate for four to six weeks, classify workloads by latency, throughput, data sensitivity, and growth trend, and identify the top three constraints. Then run a controlled experiment: batch more aggressively, cache repeated prompts, consolidate duplicate services, and right-size instances. Track cost per useful request, p50/p95 latency, GPU idle time, and failure rate. If the remaining gap is clear and durable, purchase only the capacity needed for that gap, with a review date and a resale or redeployment plan.

Bottom line: improve utilisation first, buy selectively second. This is not a frugal stance; it is a disciplined one. It protects cost, improves latency where it matters, reduces avoidable risk, and preserves optionality. If the evidence changes, we can act quickly. If it does not, we avoid locking in capacity we do not need.

Internal engineering memo: buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of what we own

To: platform and ML team
From: infrastructure review
Re: local AI capacity decision

The question is not whether the workload is growing; it is. The question is whether the next dollar should buy more accelerators, or whether we should first make the existing fleet do more useful work. My recommendation is to improve utilisation first, with a narrowly scoped hardware purchase only after the utilisation work proves the gap is real.

The cost case is uncomfortable. Local hardware has a fixed cost that is easy to underestimate: purchase price, power, cooling, rack space, maintenance, spare parts, staff time, and the opportunity cost of leaving capacity idle. If a machine sits at 20 percent average utilisation, the effective cost per useful inference is five times the sticker cost. That is not a reason to avoid hardware; it is a reason to measure it honestly. We should track not only GPU hours but useful tokens, completed jobs, successful requests, and time-to-first-token, because a busy GPU that returns low-quality or retried output is not a healthy system.

Latency matters because the product promise is interactive. If users wait seconds for a response, the model is not merely slow; it changes behaviour. Some workloads can tolerate batching and queuing, but interactive assistants, code completion, and internal copilots cannot. Improving utilisation must not mean packing requests so tightly that tail latency degrades. The right target is not maximum utilisation but high utilisation with bounded p95 and p99 latency. That means admission control, request shaping, caching, and separating latency-sensitive traffic from batch jobs.

Reliability is the other side of the same coin. More hardware can improve headroom, but it can also increase operational complexity: more drivers, more failure modes, more monitoring, more upgrades, and more places where a bad deployment can hurt many users. Better utilisation often improves reliability by reducing queues and making capacity more predictable. However, aggressive batching can create brittle dependencies if one slow tenant consumes the whole pool. We need isolation by workload class, not a single shared pool.

Opportunity cost is easy to miss. Every dollar spent on local hardware is a dollar not spent on evaluation, data quality, observability, or product features. If the bottleneck is actually poor prompts, stale embeddings, weak evaluation, or uneven traffic, buying GPUs will not fix it. Conversely, if the bottleneck is genuinely compute-bound, delaying hardware can cost revenue or slow roadmap delivery. The memo should therefore avoid a purely financial answer and ask what the team is trying to enable next quarter.

Reversibility favours the utilisation-first path. Software changes, scheduling policies, caches, and routing rules can be rolled back. Hardware purchases are harder to reverse. A new accelerator may be useful, but if demand shifts, the asset can become stranded. A leased or cloud-burst option can provide flexibility, though it may trade local control for variable cost. The best posture is reversible by default: instrument first, optimise second, buy only when the evidence is strong.

My recommendation is therefore staged. In the next four to six weeks, instrument the fleet, separate interactive from batch traffic, add caching and admission control, and publish a utilisation report by workload. In parallel, run a small pilot with a limited number of additional GPUs or a short-term burst capacity to test whether the remaining gap is real. If after that the p95 latency and queue depth still exceed targets, purchase targeted hardware sized to the proven shortfall, not to peak enthusiasm.

Uncertainty remains. Demand may grow faster than expected, or the workload mix may change. Utilisation gains may be smaller than hoped if traffic is bursty. Hardware prices and availability may move. I would not commit to a large purchase today. I would commit to the measurement and optimisation work, and to a decision gate with explicit thresholds: if utilisation rises without latency regression and the gap persists, buy; if not, do not. That is the most honest path: spend where the evidence points, keep the option to expand, and avoid paying for capacity we do not yet need.

appliance.competing_traffic: none (sq27-test stopped; a stale sglang benchmark from 11-04 stopped with the operator's approval)
appliance.drafter: DSpark (bundled mtp.safetensors), 7 draft tokens, greedy drafts; speculation with one live request (ATLAS_DFLASH_BATCH_DEPTH=1:7,1000000:0) and only while drafts pay (ATLAS_DFLASH_ADAPTIVE=1: under 2 accepted a step over 12 steps decodes plainly until a re-probe 256 tokens later)
appliance.quantisation: Spark: calibrated GPTQ NVFP4 attention, lm_head and L20-23 experts over the shipped checkpoint, for decode and verify rows; prefill reads the checkpoint's own tensors, its experts' inputs quantized as its hf_quant_config.json requires (NVFP4 / MXFP8 rows, W4A4 / W8A8)
appliance.scheduler: SparkInkling default profile: max-num-seqs 8, gpu-memory-utilization 0.80, prefill chunks 4096, CUDA graphs, programmatic dependent launch (ATLAS_INKLING2_PDL=1), prefix caching with conv-state snapshots (--enable-prefix-caching, --ssm-cache-slots=128, ATLAS_QWEN4EXP_AUX_PINNED=1), --request-timeout=3600, --tool-max-tokens=32768
